results.title: Computable: will it survive the AI era? Assessed 27 July 2026 · WillItSurvive
highlights:
Computable is a two-person team entering a GPU-hour resale market where better-funded rivals already have supply, staff, and regulated price curves live.

Computable lets people buy and sell unused hours on graphics processing chips (GPUs), similar to how you might resell concert tickets. The problem: SF Compute already raised $40 million, has 30 people, and is doing the exact same thing with more money and customers. Even harder, regulated markets like Kalshi just launched public price lists for GPU time, which means anyone can see the fair price online instead of needing Computable to tell them. Computable is a two-person team with no announced customers or deals yet. The one thing that could matter: if Computable finds a specific group of buyers or sellers that SF Compute ignores (say, companies in Asia or those who want locked-in monthly deals), they could build something real. Otherwise, the Demo Day in September will show whether they have any of that or are just copying a crowded playbook.

...

Bigger players: SF Compute. SF Compute already runs the same weekly GPU-hour resale marketplace with $100M+ hardware, 30 staff, and $40M raised at a $300M valuation. Could a giant copy it? Yes, easily.

What protects it. Hyperscalers avoid running resale markets themselves, but that gap protects every rival equally, not Computable specifically.

...

Computable's YC S26 Demo Day presentation on September 10, 2026. Whether founders reveal any traction, supply deals, or niche buyers versus generic positioning. CFTC rulings on CME/Silicon Data and ICE/Ornn cash-settled compute futures. Whether regulated forward curves commoditize the price discovery Computable relies on. SF Compute's user count or feature rollout in the 12 months after its July 2026 raise. Whether its liquidity network effect locks in the market before Computable gains any foothold.

Key numbers

- SF Compute: $40M raised at $300M valuation (2026-07-21)
- Ornn: $33M seed led by a16z crypto (2026-07-06)
- Kalshi launched CFTC GPU forward curves (2026-07-14)

...

- Regulated GPU futures from Kalshi, CME, and ICE could commoditize price-discovery value core to Computable's model. Severity: high
- No disclosed founder identity, funding, or traction creates execution and credibility uncertainty. Severity: medium
- Two-person team may lack capacity to build supply relationships or scale against 30-person competitors. Severity: medium
- No independent funding beyond YC standard investment limits runway and competitive response capacity.

Is Computable profitable in 2026?
: No revenue, customer counts, or profitability figures for Computable have been disclosed. As of July 27, 2026, its YC listing shows a 2-person team with no public financials, funding round, or named customers beyond the standard YC investment.
Who are Computable's founders?
: Computable's actual founder names are unconfirmed as of July 27, 2026. Its YC page lists Brad Flora as 'Primary Partner,' but Flora is a YC General Partner and prior founder of Perfect Audience, not a Computable founder, per his own YC bio.
Who is Computable's biggest competitor?
: SF Compute is Computable's closest direct rival, offering the same weekly GPU-hour resale marketplace. SF Compute raised $40M at a $300M valuation on July 21, 2026, with roughly 30 staff and $100M+ in managed hardware, versus Computable's 2-person team.
Could AI replace Computable?
: Computable's function is market-making for GPU-hours, not an AI-replaceable task itself, but regulated price-discovery tools like Kalshi's GPU forward curves, live since July 14, 2026, could commoditize the pricing value Computable would otherwise provide.
Who owns Computable?
: Computable is privately held and part of Y Combinator's Summer 2026 batch as of July 27, 2026. No independent funding round, valuation, or lead investor beyond YC's standard batch investment has been publicly disclosed.
Has Computable raised venture funding?

results.title: What the 2026 GPU Capacity Crunch Did to Rental Prices | AI Compute Marketplace | Compare GPU Cloud & Data Centers | ComputeStacker Insights
results.author: Tasha Nishid
highlights:
## What the 2026 GPU capacity crunch did to rental prices

The numbers tell it simply-

| GPU | Mid-2026 rate | The move |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H100 (1-year contract) | ~$2.35/hr | up ~40% since October 2025 |
| H200 | ~$2.80/hr | climbing steadily |
| B200 (Blackwell) | ~$4.90 to $5.64/hr | up 48% in 60 days, roughly doubled |
| B300 | ~$5.29/hr | new premium tier |
| GB300 | ~$5.88/hr | scarcest and priciest |

Older and newer GPUs alike climbed through 2026, the opposite of how hardware usually ages.

Our story starts with the H100, which is just the beginning. The price for 1-year contracts on the H100 rose by 40%, reaching the level of $2.35 per hour in March compared to $1.70 per hour in October. An increase in prices for the outdated processor of two generations back. However, it happens only if there is more demand than supply for the entire stack, not just the top end.

The madness at the top end was even more impressive. The spot rental price on the Blackwell was as high as $4.08 per GPU hour in April, increasing 48% from $2.75 two months earlier, which attracted so much attention that it was mentioned in the Bloomberg Terminal. In July, the price of the B200 tier rose from $3.81 to $5.64. Meanwhile, the price on the Blackwell services increased nearly three times, compared to the previous record of the H100 processor.

Thus, in conclusion, we can say that prices have doubled since January.

## What made it happen: three bottlenecks, a stampede, and everything else going wrong.

But that’s not one bottleneck. That’s three of them happening simultaneously, alongside with the increase in demand.

Packaging. Advanced GPUs need to have the memory attached through CoWoS technology provided by TSMC. And there is no room left whatsoever, none, zero, the calendar is completely booked up at least until mid-2027, which is the absolute maximum limit of accelerators to be physically manufactured. Nothing can be done about it.

Memory. Even more crucial than packaging. Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have started allocating capacities for the production of memory not for their standard DDR5 and NAND, but for HBM required for AI processors, and HBM3e prices have increased by around 20% in terms of 2026 contracts. AI initiatives are projected to consume up to 40% of global DRAM output. High prices of memory lead to high prices of the entire GPU, regardless of whether the manufacturer had some memory in stock.

Power and cooling. Blackwell GPUs require lots of power and liquid cooling infrastructure, which is not always provided by modern datacenters. Some hyperscalers have Blackwell GPUs already bought, but they are just unable to use them due to insufficient power and memory.

And then came the stampede. Demand surged for inference, not just training. NVIDIA quietly moved its wafer production from H100 to the more profitable Blackwell, which created an even scarcer supply of H100. On top of that, the huge hyperscaler orders that were worth billions of dollars exhausted the rest of NVIDIA’s allocation.

...

The war was won on price through pricing power. Short-term contracts were put secondary or even pre-emptable, payment was made upfront, and access to capacity required financial commitment. CoreWeave has hiked spot rates more than 20% since December 2025 and started pressuring small customers to enter three-year contracts.

Here is the way the crunch works. It’s not just about hourly prices. The inflexible commitment-oriented approach to cloud GPU rental that used to be the unique feature of the technology is slowly taken away from everyone without any forward commitment contract.

The impact went even to the labs. Outages occurred due to shortages at Anthropic, and OpenAI reduced its product portfolio in an attempt to decrease inference loads. And since they are squeezed, we all are squeezed.

...

The bearish sentiment regarding the situation centers around timing. HBM and CoWoS shortages are going to last at least until the first six months of 2027, whereas H100 and H200 prices are not going to drop until additional memory capacity becomes available somewhere around the end of 2026 and beginning of 2027.

results.title: DigitalOcean (NYSE: DOCN) Raises On-Demand GPU Prices by Roughly 30% Starting August 1
results.author: Nitish Kishor
highlights:
Key Highlights

- DigitalOcean is raising on-demand prices for select Nvidia and AMD GPUs by roughly 30%, effective August 1.
- H100 pricing will increase from $3.39 to $4.41 per hour.
- H200 pricing will rise from $3.44 to $4.47 per hour, and AMD's MI300X from $1.99 to $2.59.
- Existing reserved contracts keep current rates until renewal; new and renewed 12-month plans move to the higher pricing.

DigitalOcean ($DOCN) is raising on-demand prices for select Nvidia and AMD graphics processing units by roughly 30%, starting August 1, citing strong demand for advanced AI compute.

## What Happened

Under the new pricing, on-demand access to Nvidia's H100 chip will increase from $3.39 to $4.41 per hour. The H200, Nvidia's more advanced successor chip, will rise from $3.44 to $4.47 per hour.

AMD's MI300X accelerator will see its on-demand rate increase from $1.99 to $2.59 per hour, a comparable percentage increase to the two Nvidia chips.

The company said the price increases are being driven by strong demand for advanced AI compute capacity.

## Market Reaction

Existing reserved contracts will keep their current rates until renewal, meaning customers already locked into reserved pricing agreements will not see an immediate cost increase.

New and renewed 12-month plans, however, will move to the higher pricing, extending the roughly 30% increase beyond on-demand usage to longer-term commitments signed or renewed after the change takes effect.

...

The August 1 effective date gives existing on-demand customers a defined window before the new rates take hold, while the shift for new and renewed 12-month plans suggests the higher pricing is intended to apply broadly across DigitalOcean's GPU compute offerings going forward.

results.title: The compute market publishes prices. It often withholds the inputs needed to interpret them. | Daniel Kaufman
results.author: Daniel Kaufman
highlights:
The compute market publishes prices. It often withholds the inputs needed to interpret them.
Three pieces tested that problem. Each found a different constraint.
1 — The most disclosed compute index sits outside the regulatory perimeter.
Inferra combines four roles: rental market, derivatives venue, index administrator and settlement-token issuer.
Yet it discloses more construction detail than any of the four CFTC-track providers in my catalogue: primary input, outlier filtering, smoothing, a stale-data rule and a 20% cap on its own trade weight.
That cap is the only quantified public limit on self-reference among the five administrators. But the parameters, source list and full calculation remain unpublished.
The reported output may be verifiable. The calculation is not reproducible.
2 — Remove index basis and the spread is still unreadable.
Kalshi and Polymarket both list GPU rental price contracts, and both contract texts name the same Ornn dashboard URL for settlement.
Index basis: zero.
But the headline $2.17 B200 gap compares an American touch barrier with a terminal bracket—different payoffs, not different views. Match touch with touch and the gap falls to $0.10, below the $0.31 bid-ask band on the Kalshi leg alone.
In these thin markets, the quotes also fail consistency checks: a six-bracket partition sums to 180%; a survival function is non-monotone.
Disclosure was necessary. It was not the constraint.
3 — When nobody publishes the number, measure it.
On July 30, a frontier lab cut one model tier’s published price 80%. Meanwhile, a US East neocloud H100 quote roughly doubled from its Q3 2025 trough, while hyperscaler H100 quotes fell 26–54% from Q1 2025 to Q3 2026.
Write this as an inference spark spread—token price minus GPU cost adjusted for serving efficiency—and one unpublished term remains: tokens per GPU-hour.
I computed it from 1,024 vLLM runs on Llama-3.1-70B joined to CC-BY national-lab power traces.
At saturation: 11.6M tokens per GPU-hour and 51 Wh per million tokens.
The new card raises required break-even efficiency 5×. The middle and flagship tiers remain comfortably above it; the lowest tier lands near the bound. That says something about model class, not anyone’s realized margins.
Three questions. Three answers:
• Publish the methodology.
• Match the payoff before reading the spread.
• Measure the engineering term directly.
Research + tools:
Verifiable is not replicable
https://lnkd.in/gTsdC9j2
Two venues, one index
https://lnkd.in/gwWb9JV7
The inference spark spread
https://lnkd.in/gSDND599
Administrator catalogue
https://lnkd.in/g6hFjQK4
Which should the market standardize first: methodology, payoff or tokens per GPU-hour?

results.title: Ornn Raises $33M to Turn GPU Compute into a Tradable Commodity
results.author: Nexi.fund Labs
highlights:
Ornn, a startup founded by MIT alumni, raised $33 million in seed funding led by Andreessen Horowitz to build a marketplace where GPU compute is traded like a commodity. The Ornn Compute Price Index (OCPI) is already live on the Bloomberg Terminal, tracking spot prices for Nvidia H100, H200, and B200 chips based on real transactions. In May, Intercontinental Exchange, the parent of the New York Stock Exchange, announced plans to launch cash-settled GPU compute futures referenced to the OCPI. Regulatory approval is pending.

...

According to its data, the Nvidia Blackwell spot rental price surged 48% between mid-February and mid-April 2026, from $2.75 to $4.08 per GPU-hour. Consider a company that committed to a six-month training run in February. If it got priced on the April index, its largest single cost line increased by nearly half. No warning. No hedging option.

results.title: AWS cuts costs for H100, H200, and A100 instances by up to 45% - DCD
results.author: Georgia Butler
highlights:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) has significantly reduced costs for accessing Nvidia H100 and A100 GPUs on its platform.

Revealed by the company on June 5, the price reductions have applied to on-demand purchases since June 1, and to Savings Plans purchases after June 4.

 

 – Getty Images 

The instances impacted are the P4d (A100), P4de (A100), P5 (H100), and P5en (H200).

The on-demand price reduction is 33 percent for A100s across both instance types, 25 percent for the H200 instance type, and 44 percent for the H100 instance.

The 'Savings Plans' cost reduction varies from 25 percent in three years, to 45 percent in three years.

AWS offers two Savings Plans - EC2 Instance and Compute. The former offers the lowest prices in exchange for commitment to use of instances in a Region, while the latter is more flexible regardless of instance type and location. The company has also made the B200 P6 instances available through savings plans.

In a blog post, AWS explained: "Regular price reductions on AWS services have been a standard way for AWS to pass on the economic efficiencies gained from our scale back to our customers."

The company added that high demand for GPU capacity has historically outpaced industry-wide supply, making GPUs more expensive to access.

While AWS puts this reduction down to economies of scale, DCD has previously spoken to Ditlev Bredahl, CEO of host.AI, a company offering a GPU orchestration platform to help GPUaaS providers, who had some concerns about the ongoing economics of GPUs.

“A year ago or so, an H100 was maybe $5-6 per hour. Now, it's around 75 cents, maybe less. Hardware typically depreciates in three to five years, but that's happening in a year now," Bredahl told DCD, though noted that this was more of an issue for neoclouds who have a "one-to-one relationship between the rental property and the customer.”

results.title: Is AI Computing Power Becoming a Commodity?
results.author: Antti Belt, Allen Thomas
highlights:
Those long-term contracts also help address price risk. According to the Silicon Data H100 rental index, the price of an H100 GPU has risen about 2.2% per month since January 2025. Over that same period, prices fell by as much as 11% at one point and rose to roughly 25% above their starting level at another.

...

## Headwinds to the Development of a Liquid AI Computing Power Market

Companies have made some moves to evolve the market. Amazon Web Services, for example, launched EC2 Spot Instances in 2009 as a bidding market for unused capacity, but it later shifted to a model based on long-term supply and demand for spare capacity. More recently, independent venues such as SF Compute have pushed the idea further by building a marketplace for GPU clusters with resale built in.

However, several factors have made such efforts—and the overall shift toward a more efficient market—challenging: 

- Technical Complexity. AI compute differs along three dimensions. First, it can be cheaper or more available at certain times (for example off-peak hours, periods of low demand, seasonal lulls, or demand spikes immediately after the launch of a new AI model). Second, it can vary in quality. An H100 does not deliver the same performance as an H200. And non-GPU expenses such as CPU computing power, networking, storage, orchestration software, and support are often hidden, as are provider-specific factors such as downtime, setup time, debugging time, and the performance tuning required for networking and storage. Third, AI compute costs and availability differ by geographic location. (See Exhibit 4.)
- Lack of Consensus Benchmarks. A trusted benchmark for AI compute would enable all players across the ecosystem to compare offers, evaluate GPU-backed assets, or build the financial products to hedge price risk. In mature commodity markets such as oil, benchmarks may differ but they still give participants a common view of price. Benchmarks for AI compute are beginning to emerge, including the Ornn H100 Index and the Silicon Data H100 Rental Index, among others. But each benchmark uses a different methodology to collect data and normalize pricing on the basis of heterogeneous AI compute. As a result, the same GPU on the same day can fetch significantly different prices across indices. (See Exhibit 5.)
- Capital Availability. Although many AI labs and AI services companies are not yet highly profitable, equity funding is still available; and although debt is costly, they can often find alternatives. As a result, managing price risk has only recently become a major concern.
- Data Center Player Incentives. Data center players have historically leaned on long-term bilateral contracts and have had little reason to standardize pricing or to support open benchmarks. Going forward, however, some data center players may see strategic value in greater market transparency if it reduces their funding costs and helps them persuade enterprise customers to switch to them from competitors that price more opaquely.

results.title: Capex at the Nine Largest Cloud Service Providers Is Expected to Grow About 90% in 2026. Why Does AI ROI Remain Contentious?
results.author: 456X Semi-AI
highlights:
1. AI capex is not cooling, but the margin for error is shrinking. TrendForce expects the nine largest global cloud service providers’ capex to grow about 90% year over year in 2026, exceeding $886.7 billion; UBS expects hyperscaler capex in its sample to grow about 85% and 45% in 2026 and 2027, respectively. Spending forecasts continue to rise, but capex as a share of operating cash flow may reach 107% and 113%, naturally shifting the market’s focus from “how much they bought” to “how much they earned back.”
2. GPU rental pricing is the most useful real-time pressure gauge, but for now it is only an indicator. One market sample that did not fully disclose platforms, regions, or contract durations shows that per-GPU hourly prices for A100, H100, and B200 have risen about 23%, 25%, and 27%, respectively, since the beginning of the year. Pricing and supply are rising simultaneously, supporting the view that demand remains tight; however, only concurrent improvements in pricing, utilization, service levels, and renewal rates can prove that data-center capacity is genuinely “fully sold.”
3. Orders, sold-out capacity, and remaining performance obligations cannot be equated directly with profit. Trainium capacity has reportedly been largely sold out through the end of 2027, while some memory capacity has also been reserved in advance; Palantir’s results provide a clearer illustration of contract-quality tiers: TCV and RDV indicate potential demand, RPO reflects more stringent non-cancellable obligations, while billings, deferred revenue, and free cash flow demonstrate actual conversion.
4. AI capex is shifting the profit pool toward power, memory, packaging, networking, and testing, but each segment has different realization conditions. onsemi estimates that its content per AI rack could rise from about $15,000 currently to $115,000 under an 800V architecture by 2030; meanwhile, CoWoS capacity expansion may initially depress utilization, and long-term HBM agreements may lock in volume without securing the highest prices. The “beneficiary” label must still pass four gates: qualification, yield, utilization, and cash flow.
5. Genuine commercialization divergence has already emerged at the application layer. Palantir’s second-quarter revenue grew 93%, with an adjusted free-cash-flow margin of 63%; Wix’s revenue grew 15%, and Base44’s gross-margin outlook improved, but the core business remained under pressure, while free cash flow excluding the effects of acquisitions and restructuring fell to $61 million. Lower model costs are only the starting point; whether customers expand usage and whether contracts convert into cash ultimately determine whether infrastructure ROI can close the loop.

...

GPU rental pricing is today’s most eye-catching signal. One market sample states that the per-GPU hourly price for A100 increased from $1.30 at the beginning of the year to $1.60, H100 from $2.15 to $2.70, B200 from $4.40 to $5.60, and H200 from about $2.60 in May to about $3.00. If the methodology is consistent, this is indeed inconsistent with the claim that “supply is already materially excessive.”

...

The most valuable data are not quotes on a given day, but rental rates, utilization, and renewal rates over several consecutive quarters for the same platform, region, and service level. ROI genuinely improves only if all three curves move upward together; higher quoted prices alone may still reflect localized supply
